title: After a Surge in Rural Applicants, Elite Colleges Face an Enrollment Challenge
summary: Around a fire pit at Amherst College, prospective students from rural towns roasted marshmallows — part of a carefully designed welcome meant to convince them that an elite liberal arts college could feel like home. Jack Hancock, a senior from Milford, Pennsylvania (population 1,100), was among them. He had beaten Amherst's steep 1-in-13 acceptance odds but was still unsure about enrolling. "I was frankly sort of shocked that they cared about rural students," he said. Hancock's visit is the latest phase of a national push to diversify selective college campuses geographically. Three years ago, wealthy University of Chicago alumnus Byron Trott invested $20 million to launch the STARS College Network (Small Town and Rural Students). The network, now expanded to 32 institutions including Brown, Columbia, Dartmouth, MIT, Stanford, and Yale, has spurred a 15% increase in rural applications — over 90,000 last year. Trott's foundation recently added another $150 million to the effort. But application numbers are only half the battle. Now, STARS is focused on getting students to actually matriculate and graduate. The obstacles are formidable. A Quinnipiac University poll found rural Americans are less likely than urban or suburban residents to believe college is beneficial, and more likely to see it as having a negative effect on values. Hancock's mother, Jodi, ordered the smallest possible car decal of her older son's college logo, wary of neighbors who might see it as putting on airs. Financial concerns also loom: rural median household income is 12% below the national average. And even when students enroll, they drop out at higher rates than their suburban peers. Marjorie Betley, STARS' executive director, acknowledges that colleges have historically neglected rural communities, breeding distrust. "We haven't shown up, and we haven't shown them that we are people who you can trust," she said. The campfire at Amherst was a small step toward changing that.
why_it_matters: This story highlights inequality in access to elite education and the cultural divide between rural communities and prestigious institutions. It shows that getting into college is only part of the struggle; feeling welcome and supported is crucial, and addressing distrust can open opportunities for students who might otherwise be left out.

background_read: Amherst College (a prestigious liberal arts college in Massachusetts) is part of a group of elite schools that have historically drawn most of their students from urban and suburban areas.

The University of Chicago (a highly selective research university in Illinois) produced Byron Trott, the wealthy alumnus who funded the STARS network, recognizing that rural students were drastically underrepresented at top colleges.

Quinnipiac University (a private university in Connecticut known for its national polls) found that rural Americans are notably more skeptical of higher education's value, reflecting a cultural divide.

The STARS College Network now includes 32 institutions such as MIT, Stanford, and Yale, and has spurred a 15% increase in rural applications to over 90,000, but enrollment and graduation remain the harder challenges.

Rural schools often lack the Advanced Placement courses and dedicated college counselors that suburban schools take for granted, making the admissions process even more daunting for students like Jack Hancock.

perspectives.description: Rural students gain access to top colleges that offer life-changing education and career networks. The STARS network's $150 million commitment shows a genuine effort to bridge a long-neglected gap, and early increases in applications are encouraging.

Elite colleges have overlooked rural America for decades, and a campfire and additional funding may not overcome deep-seated cultural biases. Many rural families still view higher education as elitist or a threat to their values, and financial barriers remain stark despite aid.

The enrollment gap between rural and urban students is rooted in systemic issues like unequal school funding, limited advanced coursework, and a historic lack of outreach. Even well-funded initiatives must contend with long-term patterns of distrust and higher dropout rates among rural students.

If successful, the STARS model could diversify campuses and become a template for other underrepresented groups. Its long-term impact will depend on whether colleges sustain genuine partnerships with rural communities—not just recruit them—and whether cultural attitudes toward higher education shift.
